source.title: Unveiling the Secret Recipe: A Guide For Supervised Fine-Tuning Small LLMs
source.authors: Aldo Pareja; N. Nayak; Hao Wang; Krishnateja Killamsetty; Shivchander Sudalairaj; Wenlong Zhao; Seungwook Han; Abhishek Bhandwaldar; Guangxuan Xu; Kai Xu; Ligong Han; Luke Inglis; Akash Srivastava

record.tranche_reason: Tests how batch size and other training choices affect downstream benchmark performance in small pretrained LLMs; this is an instruction-tuning setting rather than the natural-label image and random-label classification setting in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures downstream benchmark scores and training dynamics during supervised instruction fine-tuning. It does not measure train-versus-test error, random-label fitting, width beyond interpolation, CNN-versus-fully-connected comparisons, optimizer comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. The benchmark and training-dynamics outcomes bear on generalization-related claims but do not directly measure the generalization gap specified by these versions.
record.test_reason: The fixed-sample comparisons in Appendix A.5.9 bear on V5 in a new setting: instruction fine-tuning pretrained language models. On the same stacked dataset, equal processed-sample counts imply equal epoch budgets. Batch 7,680 initially underperforms batch 3,840, then surpasses it with extended training. The equal-gradient-step peak-score comparisons alone do not test the fixed-epoch claim. A train–test error gap is not required by V5, which names held-out performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly captures the authors' conclusions: larger batches and lower learning rates improve final downstream performance but can require more training; early gradient norms and losses are proposed as performance indicators. The record's added claim that these results do not bear on the listed versions needs correction: the matched-sample learning curves bear on V5. The authors also recommend stacked training and report little benefit from warmup or learning-rate decay.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised instruction fine-tuning of pretrained 3B–7B language models on synthetic and instruction datasets; evaluates MMLU, MTBench, and other downstream benchmarks rather than train-test error on natural labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, learning rate, training strategy, learning-rate schedule, warmup steps, model family and size, and training-sample budget are varied; results vary with batch size and learning rate, and the stated early-stage dynamics correlation is reported across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower early gradient norms and higher training losses are associated with better downstream benchmark scores.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early optimization dynamics can predict downstream performance during small-language-model instruction fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: At approximately equal gradient-step budgets, larger batches achieve higher peak benchmark scores while processing more samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger batches can improve final instruction-tuning performance when allowed greater sample and compute budgets.

record.problems: The authors report a single seed due to computational constraints. Evaluation uses downstream benchmarks rather than direct train-test error measurements. The study focuses on pretrained small language models and states that findings may not generalize to larger models or other architectures. Several results are presented in figures; no uncertainty estimates are stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the reported benchmark scores and dynamics do not measure the behavior named by any claim version, including the train-test generalization gap. Figure values are not extracted as rows for this claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Optimizer comparisons; all experiments use Adam.
Training from scratch, image classifiers, systematic identification of a critical batch size, and controlled tests of learning-rate scaling, normalization, or regularization as remedies.
Dropout interventions and interactions with weight decay or augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons against norm or margin measures.
Removal of examples selected by label-memorization influence.

missing.what: Rows comparing batches 3,840 and 7,680 at matched processed-sample budgets, including the early larger-batch disadvantage and its later reversal. The blanket omission of benchmark curves overlooks their bearing on V5.
missing.locator: Appendix A.5.9, Batch Size Comparison in Stacked Training; Figure 18

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V5. Results use a single seed without reported uncertainty estimates. Gradient norms are not magnitude-aware sharpness measurements, and factual MMLU performance is not the example-specific memorization measure in V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization, natural-label held-out accuracy, chance performance, and the specified architectures and datasets.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and test error across width.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and learned sparse connections.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparisons and held-out performance under limited or broad tuning.

Large versus small batch training at fixed epoch budgets, and whether the batch effect is a train-test generalization gap. The paper compares downstream benchmark scores after approximately equal gradient steps, with unequal sample counts.
Dropout and weight-decay interventions, including their interaction with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of memorized training examples and resulting test accuracy.

relationships.condition: Granite 7B, stacked instruction tuning, batches 3,840 versus 7,680 at equal processed-sample budgets during earlier training
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; no extracted row ids. Appendix A.5.9 explicitly reports higher scores for batch 3,840 up to approximately 3.75 million samples on MMLU and 8.5 million on MTBench, showing a larger-batch penalty at matched epoch budgets.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports an early smaller-batch advantage on MMLU and MTBench in a single-seed experiment, but the comparisons remain unverified.
